title: Reputation, Money and Fairness
overview: This chapter collects short sayings on reputation, wealth, discipline and fairness, then opens a new collection of longer teachings that warn against exploiting the poor and making careless commitments.

parts.label: A good name over riches (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: A good reputation is worth more than money, and rich and poor share the same Maker, so neither stands higher before God. Sensible people see trouble coming and step aside, while careless people walk straight into it.

parts.label: Training, debt and generosity (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: Verse 6 says early training tends to shape a whole life, though like most proverbs it describes what usually happens rather than a guarantee. The next lines note that lenders hold power over borrowers, that people who rule in anger lose their power, and that those who share food with the poor are blessed.

parts.label: Mockers, excuses and exploitation (vv. 10-16)
parts.note: Remove someone who sneers at everyone and much of the fighting stops, while a lazy person invents absurd dangers, like a lion in the street, to avoid work. The rod in verse 15 reflects the physical discipline usual in that culture, and verse 16 warns that squeezing the poor or flattering the rich with gifts ends in loss.

parts.label: A new collection begins (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: A teacher urges the student to memorize these sayings so they build trust in the LORD and make the student truthful and reliable to those they serve. The Hebrew word in verse 20 is uncertain, but many scholars read "thirty sayings" and note close parallels with an Egyptian teaching text of thirty chapters.

parts.label: Defending the poor (vv. 22-23)
parts.note: Local courts met at the city gate, and the powerful are warned not to use them to crush people who cannot defend themselves. The LORD is pictured as the poor person's advocate who will turn the harm back on their attackers.

parts.label: Anger, debts and boundaries (vv. 24-29)
parts.note: Avoid hot-tempered friends because their habits rub off, and do not guarantee someone else's loan, since you could lose even your bed. Moving an old boundary stone was a quiet way to steal a neighbor's land, and skilled, careful workers end up serving kings.

think: Think of someone whose good name you respect: what do you think actually earned it?
